en: The *Sarvatantrasiddhāntapadārthalakṣaṇasaṃgraha*, composed by the mendicant Gaurīśaṅkara.
Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa! Homage to the supreme sages!
Without you I am formless; how could you exist without me?
By good fortune, you who are who you are have now been found by me; homage be to you!
I pay homage to the feet of the wise ones known as Śrī Cetanakiṅkara and Śrīmadrāmapurī, as well as those known as Śrīmaddhīrālāla.
This "Necklace Ornament for the Wise," composed by the monk Gaurīśaṅkara— who has faith as his wealth— for the sake of awakening and for the refutation of opponents, has been compiled.
"O believers, do not think 'Where is the composition of this book, and where are you?';
what does the grace of the company of the virtuous not accomplish?"—thus spoke the voice.
O wicked ones, strike at this body of mine composed of sound;
indeed, if you desire it, strike at my body made of the five elements.
Whatever herein has occurred that contradicts established authority or tenets, due to the fault of my own intellectual dullness,
may the noble-minded ones, casting aside envy and bestowing their favor, purify it.
Whether the wise should proclaim my faults or celebrate my multitude of virtues,
my mind considers them both equal and highly esteemed.
The fool considers that which he has spoken to be a hardship.
What is the use of those by whom even radiant virtues become defects— whether for one’s exaltation or for one’s disparagement here? Rather,
let there be many such by whom even a defect attains the status of a virtue.
Homage be to those virtuous people on earth, always!

Now, if it is asked: "For what purpose is this undertaking of the compendium of characteristics (*lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*), since characteristics are of no use?"—it is replied: There is indeed great utility. For instance, as it is said regarding marriage: "A groom possessing the [proper] characteristics should marry a bride possessing the [proper] characteristics," and "One who has maintained his vow of celibacy should wed a woman endowed with auspicious marks," and "The groom should be of the same caste, learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), and possessed of these very qualities. Thus, the characteristics of men and women according to the *sāmudrika* tradition are useful for marriage.
One should worship a linga that possesses the proper characteristics and abandon one that lacks them;
therefore, with every effort, one should fashion a linga endowed with the correct marks.

Since the characteristics (*liṅga-lakṣaṇa*) mentioned in such passages as these are useful for their worship and other rites, and since other characteristics are likewise applicable as far as possible, the undertaking of this compendium of characteristics is indeed justified. The utility of these characteristics was also demonstrated by the ancient masters:
"Even the seers do not reach the end of individual objects when considering them one by one;
however, the wise reach the end of perfected things through their characteristics."

Furthermore, according to the logical principle that "the establishment of a thing occurs through its definition and its means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and not by mere assertion," the definition of a category must necessarily be required. Therefore, setting aside the means of valid cognition for the moment, we shall describe the definitions.
*Akasmātva* means being dependent on no cause, or having an uncertain cause.
|| Absence of Cruelty ||
Even toward disciples and others who engage in futile disputations and the like, it is the quality of being an instructor through means other than speaking unpleasantly;
this is the state of being imperishable (*akṣaratva*).
The nature of a script is the state of being an arrangement of letters that serves as a reminder of phonemes.
[This concludes] the section on the meaning of indivisible wholes (*akhaṇḍārthatva*).

It is the state of being devoid of internal difference (*svagatabheda*) as well as difference from those of the same class (*sajātīya*) and different classes (*vijātīya*). The term "of the same class" (*sajātīya*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the Sāṅkhya concept of the Self (*ātman*); the term "different class" (*vijātīya*) is included to exclude over-extension to space (*ākāśa*). It is the state of being non-distinct (*aviśiṣṭatva*) while being manifestable by multiple non-synonymous words (*aparyāyānekaśabda*).

The element "non-distinct" (*aviśiṣṭatva*) is included to prevent over-extension to objects such as a jar (*ghaṭa*) which, though manifested by multiple non-synonymous words like "blue jar," are qualified (*viśiṣṭa*) by "blue" through identity (*tādātmya*). Likewise, the existential clause (*satyantam*) is included to eliminate over-extension to things like a jar, which are non-distinct yet manifested by multiple synonymous words (*paryāya*) such as "jar," "kalaśa," and "kumbha."
The nature of sentences whose meaning is indivisible.

It is the capacity to produce a true cognition that does not involve the apprehension of a relation (*saṃsarga*). The term "not involving the apprehension of a relation" is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to sentences such as "the king’s man," which are intent upon expressing a relation. It is the state of terminating solely in the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*); this is an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*).
An indefinable property; it consists in being concomitant while not being inherent.
[This is] Akhyāti.

A single cognition [is defined as] one in which there is no apprehension of a difference between its own nature (*svarūpa*) and its object (*viṣaya*). The term "own nature" (*svarūpa*) is included to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to multiple cognitions having a single object; the qualifier "object" (*viṣaya*) is included to avoid over-extension to a collective cognition (*samūhālambana-jñāna*); and the phrase "of the manifestation itself" (*khyāter eva*) means "of the erroneous cognition itself.
[This concludes the section on] the fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*).
The oblation to be performed in the evening and in the morning once the fires have been established is called *aghaṭakatva*.
Subsidiary status (*aṅgatva*) consists in having as its object that which does not pervade the object-domain of that [principal].

The state of being an auxiliary (*upakārakatva*) consists in: (1) being a producer of the operation that generates the primary fruit of that [principal action], while (2) not itself generating that primary fruit. The phrase "being a producer of the operation" is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to objects such as a jar. Its utility for the knowledge of the meaning of the Veda constitutes its status as an *ajahallakṣaṇā* (non-abandoning secondary indication).

Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is the occurrence of a word in another sense related to its primary meaning without abandoning that primary meaning; for example, in the sentence "The red one runs" (*śoṇo dhāvati*), the word *śoṇa* refers to a substance such as a horse qualified by the quality of redness. The phrase "without abandoning the primary meaning" is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the case of "indication with abandonment" (*jahallakṣaṇā*). Indication is that which causes the cognition of both the indicated object and the primary meaning by way of the form that delimits the status of being the indicated object.
[End of section on] Ignorance (*ajñatva*).
It is either the state of not having studied the scriptures from the mouth of a guru, or being devoid of self-knowledge. One who knows the self is "jña"; one who is not such is "ajña.
This is ignorance (*ajñāna*).

It is that which, while being the material cause of all effects, is indefinable as either existent or non-existent; it is that which, while being an unbeginning positive entity, is removable by knowledge. The term "unbeginning" (anādi) is used to exclude prior cognitions that are removed by subsequent cognitions; the term "positive entity" (bhāvarūpa) is used to exclude antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva), or to dispel the doubt that ignorance might be merely the absence of knowledge; and the term "removable by knowledge" is used to exclude the Self from over-extension. Thus, it is the state of being directly removable by knowledge while possessing falsity.

To one who asserts that the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of desire is directly sublated by knowledge, [the author] states "directly" (*sākṣāt*). This is to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to bondage—which is sublatable by knowledge through the medium of the cessation of ignorance—for which the truth-qualification (*satyatva*) is intended. "Falsity" (*mithyātva*) is defined as being a beginningless material cause (*anādyupādānatva*). The term "falsity" is used to exclude Brahman; "beginningless" is used to exclude clay and the like; and "being a material cause" is used to exclude the relationship between ignorance (*avidyā*) and the Self (*ātman*).
[This concludes] the section on the refutation of ignorance (*ajñānanigrahasthāna*).
Non-comprehension is the failure of the opponent to understand the meaning of a statement, even after it has been stated three times by the proponent and understood by the assembly.
This constitutes "insignificance" (*aṇutva*).
The state of being an initiator [of a composite] exists when there is the nature of a subtle substance.
[End of section. *Atikramaṇa*.
The performance of more than what is customary. || Guest ||
A person who has come to one's house and whose arrival was not previously known. || This is an extended application (atideśa). ||
Teaching concerning another subject by overstepping one's own proper domain; connecting that which was heard in one place with something else;
this is *atiprasaṅga* (an over-extension of the argument).

Ativāda (Excessive Assertion) is the consequence that if cognition occurs for one thing where it is intended, it would follow that cognition would also occur for something else; or, it is the application [of a property] to something other than the subject under discussion.
Meaningless prattle is [the definition of] excessive pervasion (*ativyāpti*).

The state of being an excellence (*atiśayatāpa*) consists in residing in the object to be defined (*lakṣya*) while not residing in that which is not the object to be defined (*alakṣya*), just as having horns (*śṛṅgitva*) is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of a cow; it resides in the cow, which is the object to be defined, while not residing in non-objects such as buffaloes.
The distress arising from perceiving the superiority of a deity greater than one's own is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole).
The reversal of the sequence [of causes and effects];

supersensuousness; the state of being a quality inherent in something other than that which possesses the property of *saṃskāra* (latent impression), which is a subordinate resident within the category of "quality" (*guṇatva*) that is the object of ordinary worldly perception;
and absolute cessation.

Absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) is either the cessation of an effect together with its cause, or that which exists in a locus not co-located with the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) belonging to the same class as its own counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).

Non-existence (abhāva) is that whose counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) is delimited by a relation existing across the three periods of time; for example, "there is no jar on the ground. The term "across the three periods of time" (traikālika) is used to exclude destruction (dhvaṃsa) and prior non-existence (prāgabhāva), while the phrase "delimited by a relation" (saṃsargāvacchinna) and so forth is used to exclude difference (bheda). This constitutes "unseen-ness" (adṛṣṭatva).
The extraordinary (*adbhuta*) is that which is beyond the senses while being produced by injunctions and prohibitions.

The connection of an established subject with the constituent parts of another subject; an operation that produces wonder; or, while being manifested by states such as startledness, being accompanied by transitory emotions (*saṃcārībhāva*) such as joy. This is non-duality (*advaitatva*).
The state of being devoid of internal differentiation as well as homogeneous and heterogeneous differentiation is "inferiority" (adhamatva).
According to the *Rasamañjarī*, it consists of being devoid of fear, compassion, and shame, and lacking discrimination between what ought and ought not to be done regarding sexual dalliance;
this is *adharma*.

[The definition of sin is: being that which produces hell, which is produced by actions prohibited by the Vedas and so forth; or, it is the demerit (pāpa) produced by actions prohibited by the Vedas and so forth. [Alternatively, it is] the state of being a means to an undesirable result as taught by the Vedas. The term "Veda" is included to exclude [acts such as] consuming poison and the like. The term "undesirable" (aniṣṭa) is included to exclude [rituals such as] the Brahma-sacrifice (brahmayāga). [End of excerpt.]
The statement of an excessive reason and so forth; the state of exceeding the appropriate measure. || Topic ||

The substratum of action, whether directly or through a succession, is the locus of the operation that results in a fruit by means of the agent and the object, as in the example: "He cooks rice in a pot at home. Logic (*nyāya*) consists of the inquiry into the Vedas. They know that a topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) in a treatise has five members: the subject matter (*viṣaya*), the doubt (*saṃśaya*), the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the rejoinder (*uttara*), and the final conclusion (*nirṇaya*).
The Section on Authority.

Those learned in the *Dharmaśāstra* maintain that [the definition of ownership] consists in a continuous succession, the status of being both the agent of action and the enjoyer of its fruit, and the state of proprietorship (*svāmitva*) which brings about the capacity to perform acts such as buying and selling according to one’s will. Grammarians (*Vaiyākaraṇas*) hold that it is the capacity to generate a comprehension of the sentence-meaning in another country, while not generating such a comprehension of the sentence-meaning in one’s own country, provided that it is applicable to the refinement of the object to be marked (*lakṣya-saṃskāra*). It is the fruit of powerful *prārabdha-karma* (commenced karma) that initiates multiple bodies.
This is the *adhikāra-vidhi* (injunction of qualification).
The injunction is the connection of the result with the instrument—such as a sacrifice—which has its duty [of performance] established, as in: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice.
[This concerns] the qualified person (*adhikārin*).

One who desires the attainment of primary and secondary purposes; one who possesses the desire for the fruits produced by various respective actions; one who possesses the fitness for performing those respective actions; one who, being free from impurity and distraction and being endowed with the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*), possesses knowledge of one's own true nature;
[this is] presiding authority (*adhiṣṭhātṛtva*).
The presiding authority over various ritual acts belongs to those respective objects merely by their presence.
This is the section on "Presiding Authority" (adhiṣṭhāna).

That which, having been superimposed upon its substrate, appears— namely, that which bestows existence and manifestation, or which is the object of ignorance accompanied by its manifestations, or even that which is the substrate of effects sublated by one's own intellect— this is the study [of the substrate].

The Vedists maintain that it is merely the recitation of the syllables; the Mīmāṃsakas hold that it is the grasping of the syllables along with their meaning. Superimposition (*adhyastatva*) consists in the utterance by a subsequent disciple occurring while the utterance from the mouth of a preceding teacher exists.
Internal-ness (*ādhyātmatva*) is the state of being distinct from recognition while being produced by the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) of conjunction (*saṃprayoga*).
The state of being concerned with the self— whether understood as the body, the senses, and so forth, as the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), or as Brahman—
is what constitutes the nature of a treatise on the inner self (*adhyātma-śāstra*).
The treatise has proceeded with reference to the self.
[This concludes] the section on superimposition (adhyāropa).
Superimposition is the attribution of a non-existent thing to a real object, such as the superimposition of silver upon a fragment of mother-of-pearl and the like. This is *adhyāsa*.

"Appearance elsewhere" (paratrāvabhāsaḥ). According to the *Parimala*, this means "an appearance whose ontological status is different from that of its substratum. It is an appearance, delimited by a single location, in that which is being conjoined with itself and yet possesses the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of that thing. If one were to state only "an appearance in that which possesses its absolute non-existence," there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to a case such as a jar that was previously removed from a spot like the ground and then brought back again; therefore, the phrase "being conjoined with itself" is stated.

Even so, since conjunction appears as being conjoined with a branch-tip on a tree that possesses the absolute absence of conjunction with a monkey at its root, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of the definition to that case; therefore, it is stated "by a single delimitation" (ekāvacchedena). [The definition of error is: being produced by a defect, while being produced by the cognition of the general nature of the substrate.

"In the *Tattvaviveka*, it is stated: 'The state of being perceived in the locus of the absolute non-existence of itself, as delimited by its ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*). This superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is of two kinds: superimposition from cognition (*jñāna-adhyāsa*) and superimposition from object (*artha-adhyāsa*). Alternatively, superimposition is twofold: superimposition of essential nature (*svarūpa-adhyāsa*) and superimposition of relation (*saṃsarga-adhyāsa*). Among these, the first is the superimposition of a snake upon a rope, or the superimposition of the non-self upon the Self."

The second [type of superimposition], however, occurs in the case of redness in a crystal, yellowness in a conch shell, and the self and its attributes in what is not the self; for there is no superimposition of the self and so forth upon their own nature by way of ultimate reality. Alternatively, superimposition is twofold based on the distinction between being "with an adjunct" (*sopādhika*) and "without an adjunct" (*nirupādhika*). Each of these two types is further divided into two kinds based on the distinction between external and internal. Among these, the error involving a red crystal and the like is an external superimposition with an adjunct, because the hibiscus flower and so forth serve as the adjunct.

The delusion of agency and so forth is internal, because it is an effect of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of ignorance (*avidyā*) which has transformed into the form of action (*karma*). On the other hand, the delusion of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like is external and without a limiting adjunct (*nirupādhika*). The delusion regarding space and so forth is also external and without a limiting adjunct. The internal delusion without a limiting adjunct includes such instances as "I am ignorant" and "I do not know Brahman. These and others should be understood in this manner. The detailed exposition, however, must be learned from the mouth of the Guru. [End of] *Adhyāhāra*.
It is a recourse when there is no other way; it is the postulation of words useful for the context at hand, or the connection of words as they are heard.
This constitutes the office of the Adhvaryu priest.
The state of being the agent of the commencement and completion of an action.
[This leads to] infinite regress.

The stream of the proven and the prover is without beginning. The term "without beginning" is used to exclude the fallacy of circularity (*cakraka*), while the phrase "proven and prover" is used to avoid the charge of mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣyatā*).
